Under the Civil Procedure Code (consolidated to Act No. 43 of 2024), section 70, an order granting leave to serve summons outside Sri Lanka must direct the defendant to file his answer **on or before the date specified in the summons**. That date must be **no later than six months from the date of the order for service outside Sri Lanka**.

Yes.  
Under **Section 71A of the Civil Procedure Code (consolidated to Act No. 43 of 2024, section‑merged)**, the court may, in addition to the ordinary service of documents, direct the Registrar to communicate any order of court—including an enjoining order, an injunction, an interim injunction, a sequestration order and an interim order—to the parties concerned by way of electronic or telephone devices.

If a defendant admits the plaintiff’s claim, the court may adjudicate the title to the thing claimed.  
This is set out in the Civil Procedure Code (consolidated to Act No. 43 of 2024, section‑merged) under the procedure at the hearing (see the passage that allows the court to “adjudicate upon the title to the thing claimed” when admissions of the parties or other evidence enable it).

Yes.  
Under the Civil Procedure Code (consolidated to Act No. 43 of 2024) a defendant’s answer to a plaint must be in writing and delivered to the court.  
- Section 73 states that the defendant (or his registered attorney) must “deliver to the court a duly stamped written answer.”  
- Section 75 further requires that every such answer be “distinctly written upon good and suitable paper, shall be duly stamped, shall be subscribed by the defendant or his duly constituted representative…”  

Thus, a written answer is mandatory.

Under the Civil Procedure Code (consolidated to Act No. 43 of 2024), a defendant who wishes to challenge the court’s jurisdiction must do so by filing a **separate and distinct plea that expressly traverses the averment of jurisdiction in the plaint**. This plea must be made independently of the main answer to the complaint.

Under the Civil Procedure Code (consolidated to Act No. 43 of 2024), if a defendant’s answer is found to be **substantially defective** (e.g., missing particulars, argumentative, prolix, or irrelevant), the court may:

1. **Reject the answer** or return it to the defendant for amendment within a period not exceeding one month from the date of return.  
2. The court may impose costs or other terms it deems appropriate.  
3. If the answer is rejected or the defendant fails to amend it within the prescribed period, the defendant is treated as having **failed to file an answer**.  
4. The court’s order must specify the grounds for rejection, and a copy of the answer is served on the plaintiff or the plaintiff’s registered attorney.  

(See Civil Procedure Code, section 77 and accompanying procedural provisions.)

Yes.  
Under the Civil Procedure Code (consolidated to Act No. 43 of 2024), the application for execution of a decree **must be in writing** (signed by the applicant or his registered attorney) and must contain the particulars listed in the code.

A party must file the notice of appeal with the original court within **fourteen days** from the date the decree or order was pronounced (exclusive of that day, the day the petition is presented, Sundays, and public holidays).  
*Source: Civil Procedure Code (consolidated to Act No. 43 of 2024, section‑merged).*

The burden of proof in a civil suit or proceeding lies on the person who would fail if no evidence were given on either side. In other words, it is on the party who asserts the facts that the court must prove those facts exist (Evidence Ordinance, Chapter 14, § 102; see also § 101).

Yes.  
Under the Evidence Ordinance, Chapter 14 (consolidated to 2024), section 114, a court may presume the existence of any fact that it thinks likely to have happened, taking into account the common course of natural events, human conduct, and public and private business as they relate to the case.

No.  
Under the Evidence Ordinance (Chapter 14) all persons are deemed competent to testify **unless** the Court finds that they are prevented from understanding the questions or from giving rational answers because of tender years, extreme old age, disease (of body or mind), unsoundness of mind, or any other similar cause.  

*Evidence Ordinance, Chapter 14 – “All persons shall be competent to testify unless the Court considers that they are prevented from understanding the questions put to them, or from giving rational answers to those questions, by tender years, extreme old age, disease, whether of body or mind, or any other cause of the same kind.”*

No.  
Under the Evidence Ordinance, Chapter 14, Section 121, a judge or magistrate may not be compelled to answer any questions about his own conduct in court (or about matters that came to his knowledge while acting as judge or magistrate) unless a judge of a superior court issues a special order. He may, however, be examined on other matters that occurred in his presence while he was acting.

A District Court has territorial jurisdiction over a civil action only if the action falls within the **local limits of that court**.  
Under the Civil Procedure Code (consolidated to Act No. 43 of 2024, section‑merged) it is stated that:

> “When it is alleged to be uncertain within the local limits of the jurisdiction of which of two or more courts any immovable property is situated, any one of those courts may, if satisfied that there is ground for the alleged uncertainty, record a statement to that effect, and thereupon proceed to entertain and dispose of any action relating to that property; and its decree in the action shall have the same effect as if the property were situated within the local limits of its jurisdiction: **Provided that the action is one with respect to which the court is competent as regards the nature and value of the action to exercise jurisdiction**.”  

Thus, the determining factors are:

1. **The local limits of the District Court** (i.e., the district in which the action is brought or the immovable property is situated).  
2. **The court’s competence in terms of the nature and value of the action**.

These provisions are found in the Civil Procedure Code (consolidated to Act No. 43 of 2024, section‑merged).

Under the Interpretation Ordinance, the term “month” means a **calendar month**, unless words are added indicating that lunar months are intended. This definition applies to Sri Lankan written law unless the law itself specifies otherwise. (Interpretation Ordinance)

Under the Interpretation Ordinance, if the last day of a prescribed time for doing an act in court falls on a day when the court is closed, the act is deemed to be done in time if it is performed on the next day thereafter on which the court is open【Interpretation Ordinance, § 8(1)】.

Under the Supreme Court Rules (incorporating amendments up to 2022), including the Court of Appeal (Appellate Procedure) Rules 1990, an application or appeal may be treated as **urgent** for a digital virtual hearing when:

* The Judge of the Court of Appeal designated for the matter by the President of the Court of Appeal **deems the application or appeal urgent**; and  
* The Judge has considered that the **inability to hold a conventional physical hearing** is due to a reason that is prejudicial to national security, public safety, or the order and security within the precincts of the Court of Appeal, **and** that there is a need to ensure the smooth and uninterrupted administration of justice.

This is set out in rule 3 of the Court of Appeal (Appellate Procedure) Rules 1990.

The Civil Procedure Code (Amendment) Act No. 4 of 2005 amended section 544 of the Civil Procedure Code by:

1. **Substituting the wording in paragraph (e)** of subsection (1) of section 544 – the phrase “within the meaning of the Banking Act, No. 30 of 1988” was replaced with “within the meaning of the Banking Act, No. 30 of 1988; ” (the exact substitution is shown in the amendment text).  
2. **Adding a new paragraph (f)** immediately after paragraph (e) of subsection (1), which reads:  
   “(f) any instrument relating to any monetary interest (other than a bearer instrument or a negotiable instrument) issued by a company or other body of persons established in terms of any law for the time being in force.”  
3. **Adding definitions at the end of subsection (1)**:  
   * “instrument” means a legally enforceable agreement expressing a contractual right to the payment of money;  
   * “bearer instrument” means a negotiable instrument transferable from one person to another, upon certain conditions being met.  

These changes are recorded in the Civil Procedure Code (Amendment) Act No. 4 of 2005.

Act No. 5 of 2022 amended section 88 of the Civil Procedure Code by repealing its existing subsection (2) and replacing it with a new subsection (2). The new subsection requires that any order setting aside or refusing to set aside a judgment entered upon default must:

* accompany the facts on which it is based and specify the grounds for the decision, and  
* be liable to an appeal to the relevant High Court (as established by Article 154 P of the Constitution) upon obtaining leave from that High Court.  

(See Civil Procedure Code (Amendment) Act, No. 5 of 2022, § 88.)

Act No. 17 of 2022 inserted **Section 154A** into the Civil Procedure Code (Chapter 101).  
Section 154A provides that, notwithstanding the Evidence Ordinance, formal proof of the execution or genuineness of any deed or document required by law (except a will under the Wills Ordinance) is not required in proceedings under the Code, unless the execution or genuineness is disputed in the pleadings or the court specifically requires such proof.

The Civil Procedure Code (Amendment) Act No. 36 of 2022 repealed **Part IX A of the Civil Procedure Code**, which comprises sections 801 to 833 inclusive【Source: Civil Procedure Code (Amendment) Act No. 36 of 2022】.

Act No. 7 of 2023 inserted a new section immediately after section 431 of the Civil Procedure Code, which is to be read as **section 431A – “Commissions for Medical Examinations.”** This provision is found in the Civil Procedure Code (Amendment) Act, No. 7 of 2023.

Act No. 29 of 2023 amended subsection (1) of section 18 of the Civil Procedure Code by replacing the words **“before the hearing”** with **“before the day first fixed for the pre‑trial conference.”** (Civil Procedure Code (Amendment) Act No. 29 of 2023).

Act No. 43 of 2024 amended section 5 of the Civil Procedure Code by inserting a new definition for the word “electronic.”  The amendment states that “electronic” shall have the same meaning assigned to it by the Electronic Transactions Act, No. 19 of 2006.  (Civil Procedure Code (Amendment) Act No. 43 of 2024, § 5)

Act No. 43 of 2024 repealed the existing Section 59 of the Civil Procedure Code and substituted it with a new Section 59. The new section provides that summons shall ordinarily be served by a process server, registered post or courier service, and sets out the circumstances under which the plaintiff may wish the summons to be served otherwise (the full text is given in the amendment). This change is recorded in the Civil Procedure Code (Amendment) Act No. 43 of 2024.
The limitation period for bringing an action for loss, injury, or damage is **two years** from the time the cause of action arises, under the Prescription Ordinance (consolidated to 2024).

An action on a written promissory note or bill of exchange must be brought within **ten (10) years** (under the Prescription Ordinance, which sets a ten‑year prescription period for such instruments).

Under the Prescription Ordinance (consolidated to 2024), a defendant who has possessed the immovable property **undisturbed for ten years prior to the bringing of the claimant’s action** is entitled to a decree in his favour with costs. This period is specified in the ordinance’s provision on possession adverse to the claimant’s title.

Under the Evidence Ordinance (Chapter 14, section 76) a public officer who is in custody of a public document that a person has a right to inspect must:

* **Give the person a copy of the document on demand**;  
* **Charge the person the applicable legal fees**; and  
* **Attach a certificate at the foot of the copy stating that it is a true copy of the document (or part thereof), dated and subscribed by the officer**.  

Thus, the officer’s duty is to provide the requested copy, collect the legal fees, and certify the copy’s authenticity.

The unlimited original jurisdiction of a District Court in civil matters within its district is conferred by the **Judicature Act No. 2 of 1978 (consolidated to 2023)**, specifically under **Section 19A** which states that “Every District Court shall have cognizance of and full power to hear and …” (the section is not fully quoted in the excerpt, but it establishes the court’s full original jurisdiction).

Under the Prescription Ordinance (consolidated to 2024), an action for goods sold and delivered, or for work and labour done, must be brought within **one year** after the debt becomes due (Prescription Ordinance, Section 8).

Under the Civil Procedure Code (Amendment) Act No. 11 of 2010, section 338 was amended by substituting paragraph (b) of subsection (3) with a new definition of “legal representative”. The amended wording reads:

> “legal representative” means an executor or administrator or, in the case of an estate below the value of rupees four million, the next of kin who have **adiated** the inheritance.  
> *Provided however, that in the event of any dispute arising as to who is the legal representative.*

Thus, the Act replaced the original paragraph (b) of subsection (3) of section 338 with this definition.

Under the Civil Procedure Code (consolidated to Act No. 43 of 2024), the parties to an action are entitled to obtain a certified copy of the judgment or final decree.  The Code states that the Registrar shall issue a certified copy to each such party free of charge (Civil Procedure Code, section 205).

Act No. 20 of 2023 repealed the existing section 205 of the Civil Procedure Code and substituted it with a new section 205.  
Under the new section 205 (Civil Procedure Code (Amendment) Act No. 20 of 2023):

1. **Sub‑section (1)** – When the parties to an action apply, the Registrar shall issue one certified copy of the judgment or final decree to each party free of charge.  
2. **Sub‑section (2)** – Subject to (1), the Registrar may, upon any person’s application (with the required fee and stamps), examine and certify copies.  However, a person who is not a party to a matrimonial, adoption or custody action is generally not entitled to certified copies of the proceedings or documents of such actions, except for the judgment, order or decree; the court may direct the Registrar to issue certified copies to such a person if the court is satisfied with the applicant’s request.

Thus, the amendment changed section 205 to provide free certified copies to parties and to allow other persons to obtain certified copies under specified conditions.

**Bail procedure for a person arrested under the Code of Criminal Procedure**

Under the Civil Procedure Code (consolidated to Act No. 43 of 2024) the following steps apply when a person is arrested on a warrant issued under the Code of Criminal Procedure:

| Step | What must be done | Form / document | Source |
|------|------------------|-----------------|--------|
| 1 | The arrested person must be brought before the court that issued the warrant, in the custody of the Fiscal. | – | Civil Procedure Code, section 651 |
| 2 | The defendant may, instead of giving bail, deposit with the Fiscal or in court the sum mentioned in the warrant. Upon deposit he is discharged from custody and a minute of the same is made on the warrant. | – | Civil Procedure Code, section 652 |
| 3 | If the defendant appears before the court, he must give bail (form No. 102, First Schedule) to abide by and perform the judgment of the court, and to pay any sums awarded against him. | Form No. 102 | Civil Procedure Code, section 652 |
| 4 | If the defendant is unable or unwilling to give such bail, he shall be committed to prison (form No. 103, First Schedule) until he gives bail or until the determination of the action. | Form No. 103 | Civil Procedure Code, section 652 |
| 5 | Alternatively, the defendant may give reasonable security (form No. 101, First Schedule) to the Fiscal to appear and answer the plaintiff’s claim. | Form No. 101 | Civil Procedure Code, section 651 |

These provisions are the bail procedure applicable to a person arrested under the Code of Criminal Procedure.

Under the Civil Procedure Code (consolidated to Act No. 43 of 2024) a divorce may be granted on **any ground that, under the law applicable to Sri Lanka, renders the marriage void or allows it to be dissolved**.  
This is set out in the Code itself:  

* “Any husband or wife may present a plaint to the Family Court … praying that his or her marriage may be dissolved on **any ground for which marriage may, by the law applicable in Sri Lanka to his or her case, be dissolved**.” (Civil Procedure Code, section 597)  

* “Such decree may be made on **any ground which renders the marriage contract between the parties void by the law applicable to Sri Lanka**.” (Civil Procedure Code, section 608)  

The specific statutory grounds (e.g., adultery, desertion, cruelty, etc.) are set out in the marriage‑related statutes that apply to Sri Lanka, but those details are not provided in the excerpt supplied.

**Bail procedure for a person arrested under the Code of Criminal Procedure (CPC)**  

1. **Immediate court appearance** – The arrested person must be brought before the court that issued the warrant (the “court of the warrant”) in the custody of the Fiscal.  
   *Source: Civil Procedure Code (consolidated to Act No. 43 of 2024) – section 651.*

2. **Security or bail** – The arrested person may give the court security (bail) in the form specified in the warrant.  
   * He may deposit the sum mentioned in the warrant with the Fiscal or in court.  
   * If he gives such security, he is discharged from custody.  
   * If he does not give security, he is committed to prison.  
   *Source: Civil Procedure Code (consolidated to Act No. 43 of 2024) – sections 651 and 652.*

3. **Release on illness** – If the arrested person is seriously ill, the court may cancel the warrant and release him.  
   *Source: Civil Procedure Code (consolidated to Act No. 43 of 2024) – sections 836 and 837.*

These provisions outline the bail and release procedures applicable to a person arrested under the CPC.
